note: Refreshed every week by the program's research task. Each item says what changed, why it matters to a data engineer or architect, and how to test the claim yourself.

items.title: Claude Fable 5.2: 20% cheaper per token, and editing earlier turns before sending back a thinking block now fails
items.summary: Released on 9 November 2026. Claude Fable 5.2 (and Mythos 5.2 for verified organizations) has a 1M-token context window, 128k max output and always-on adaptive thinking, at $8 per million input and $40 per million output tokens (5.1 was $10 and $50). A fast mode gives up to 2.5x output tokens per second at $16 and $80. The prefix check is now enforced on every account: changing the system prompt, tools or earlier messages and then sending back a thinking block returns a 400. Both models need 30-day data retention.
items.why: Price per token fell, but the bigger cost lever is still the cache: a harness that rewrites its history (trims old tool results, reorders tools) now breaks loudly instead of silently missing the cache. Fast mode doubles the price for speed, so it belongs only on the latency-critical path, chosen by your gateway, not by default.
items.try: In projects/ai-foundations/labs/lab7_optimise.py, price one agent run at 5.1 and 5.2 rates, then at 5.2 fast mode. Then make lab1_loop.py trim an old tool result between turns and note which turn would now be refused; move the trimming to the end of the context so the prefix stays intact.

items.title: Self-hosted Claude Managed Agents: the whole agent service, sessions and history run on your own infrastructure
items.summary: Launched on 12 November 2026. The customer runs the entire Managed Agents service, not only the sandboxes, on its own infrastructure, and agents, sessions and session history are stored there. Model requests go to the provider you choose, Anthropic by default. Access is requested through the account team.
items.why: Session history of a data agent holds query results, table names and sometimes customer rows. Keeping the agent's state inside your own network turns 'where does agent memory live' into a normal data-residency and retention decision, owned like any other store, while only model calls leave.
items.try: For the on-call agent in lab10_oncall.py, list everything a session stores (prompts, tool calls, query results, decisions). Mark which fields could hold customer data, then write the retention rule and the store you would keep each in if the agent ran self-hosted.

items.title: Databricks: an always-on Genie that works in the background, splits work across sub-agents and stays inside Unity Catalog permissions
items.summary: Announced on 11 November 2026 as the second generation of Genie. It runs in the background on its own compute, delegates to sub-agents in parallel, and surfaces items needing attention in a priority inbox. Genie Search uses 100+ connectors: it indexes content in place, ingests through Lakeflow Connect, or queries live through MCP. Actions stay within Unity Catalog permissions and Unity Gateway approval rules and budgets.
items.why: A background agent with its own compute is a job you schedule, cap and audit. The design choice worth naming in an interview is the governance boundary: permissions come from the catalog the agent queries, and spend and approvals from the gateway, not from the prompt.
items.try: Split lab10_oncall.py into a planner and two sub-agents (logs, lineage) that run in parallel. Give the run a token budget and an approval list of actions; run lab11_eval.py and compare minutes and cost per incident with the single-agent version.

items.title: Databricks Genie Ontology is generally available: a context layer that Databricks says doubles agent pass rates at half the tokens
items.summary: Announced on 11 November 2026. Genie Ontology is GA, with Genie Search, Ontology Snippets, organizational directories (Workday first) and Unity Catalog domains, subdomains and pages. External knowledge sources (Power BI) and SharePoint search are in beta. On Databricks' own benchmark Genie passed 91% of tasks against 45% and 58% for two unnamed frontier agents, using 432K tokens a run against 889K and 1.05M.
items.why: The claim is that context, not the model, decides a data agent's accuracy and cost: definitions, owners and trusted tables cut both wrong answers and tokens. It is a vendor benchmark against unnamed agents, so treat it as a hypothesis to test on your own questions.
items.try: In lab5_evals.py, run 10 data questions twice: once with only table schemas in context, once with a short ontology (metric definitions, owners, the trusted table for each). Report pass rate and tokens per question for both.

items.title: Anthropic: Claude Data, Meetings, Sheets and Whiteboards for Claude Enterprise, with Adobe, Atlassian and HubSpot connectors
items.summary: Launched on 10 November 2026 for Claude Enterprise. Claude Data turns company data into dashboards, data stories and videos; Claude Meetings joins a video call and starts work during it; Claude Sheets and Whiteboards let teams build with the agent on shared spreadsheets and boards. New connectors cover Adobe, Atlassian and HubSpot.
items.why: When business users get dashboards straight from an agent, the data team's product becomes the governed layer underneath: certified tables, metric definitions and access rules that any agent reads. A wrong number now spreads in a meeting, not a ticket.
items.try: Pick three metrics from your lab data and write, for each, the definition, owner and trusted table an agent must use. Expose them through lab9_mcp_server.py as a describe_metric tool and check with lab9_client.py that an answer cites it.
